title: ABIMELECH TOOK SARAH—THEN GOD CLOSED EVERY WOMB IN HIS HOUSEHOLD
paragraphs: ABIMELECH TOOK SARAH—THEN GOD CLOSED EVERY WOMB IN HIS HOUSEHOLD

He thought he had taken another woman into his palace. He did not realize he had stepped into a promise God Himself was guarding—and what happened next reveals something terrifying about sin, breathtaking about grace, and ultimately points us toward Jesus Christ.
There are moments in Scripture that make you stop reading.
Not because the words are difficult.
Because suddenly you realize how seriously God takes things we have learned to treat casually.
Genesis 20 contains one of those moments.
A king saw Sarah.
A king took Sarah.
And then something happened throughout his household.
Wombs closed.
Life stopped being conceived.
The future of an entire household was suddenly placed under divine restraint.
And perhaps the most unsettling part of the story is this:
Abimelech had not even slept with her.
Not yet.
That matters.
Because this story is not simply about what a man did.
It is about what God prevented him from doing.
And if you have ever wondered whether God has protected you from sins you never knew you were capable of committing, you may never read this chapter the same way again.
Abraham had traveled into the territory of Gerar. He was carrying extraordinary promises from God, yet he was still capable of very ordinary fear.
That should humble every believer.
You can have faith and still become afraid.
You can have encountered God and still make terrible decisions.
You can know His promises and still panic when circumstances make those promises appear vulnerable.
Abraham feared that men might kill him because of Sarah’s beauty. So Sarah was presented as his sister.
There was truth buried inside the statement—Genesis 20:12 explains their familial relationship—but the arrangement concealed the most important truth relevant to the situation:
Sarah was Abraham’s wife.
Then Scripture records the moment with frightening simplicity:
“Abimelech king of Gerar sent, and took Sarah.”
The Hebrew is brutally uncomplicated:
וַיִּקַּח אֶת־שָׂרָה
wayyiqqaḥ ’et-Sarah.
“And he took Sarah.”
A few words.
An enormous crisis.
Because Sarah was not merely Abraham’s wife.
She stood inside the unfolding covenant promise.
God had already declared that Sarah would bear Abraham a son. Through Isaac the covenant line would continue.
So imagine the apparent catastrophe.
The woman God promised would become the mother of Isaac is now inside another man’s household.
Abraham’s fear has created a mess.
Sarah is vulnerable.
Abimelech believes he is acting within what has been represented to him.
And from a human perspective, everything appears dangerously close to unraveling.
But heaven has not lost control.
That sentence may be for someone reading this with trembling hands.
Heaven has not lost control.
Not over your family.
Not over your failure.
Not over the consequences frightening you tonight.
Not over the chapter you wish you could erase.
Abraham's mistake did not cancel God's sovereignty.
And your failure has never made God confused about what to do next.
That does not make sin harmless.
Genesis 20 proves precisely the opposite.
God came to Abimelech in a dream.
And there was no polite introduction.
God essentially announced that death stood before him because the woman he had taken was married.
Abimelech protested that he had acted with integrity.
He had been told she was Abraham's sister.
Sarah herself had participated in the representation.
Then God said something astonishing.
He acknowledged Abimelech's integrity in the matter—and then revealed something Abimelech could never have known.
God had restrained him.
Genesis 20:6 says, in substance, that God had kept Abimelech from sinning against Him and therefore had not allowed him to touch Sarah.
Think about that.
Abimelech could say, “I didn't touch her.”
God could say, in effect:
Because I stopped you.
That should dismantle some of our pride.
How many times have we congratulated ourselves for sins we never committed when perhaps God quietly removed the opportunity?
How many relationships never happened because God knew where they would lead?
How many doors slammed shut while we accused God of abandoning us?
How many plans collapsed because mercy stood in the doorway and said, “You cannot go any farther”?
Sometimes grace feels like an open door.
Sometimes grace feels like a closed one.
Sometimes God's mercy gives you what you prayed for.
Sometimes His mercy refuses to let you have what would destroy you.
And sometimes the greatest miracle in your testimony is something you will never know happened because God prevented it before it became your story.
Abimelech was commanded to return Sarah.
Then God identified Abraham as a prophet and instructed that Abraham would pray for him.
There is uncomfortable grace everywhere in this chapter.
Abraham had behaved fearfully.
Yet God had not discarded Abraham.
Abimelech had taken another man's wife.
Yet God warned Abimelech before the situation progressed and provided a path toward restoration.
Sarah had been placed in an extraordinarily vulnerable situation.
Yet God Himself intervened.
Nobody in Genesis 20 gets to boast.
And maybe that is exactly the point.
The hero of Genesis 20 is not Abraham.
It is not Abimelech.
It is not human wisdom.
It is God.
The God who warns.
The God who restrains.
The God who protects.
The God who exposes.
The God who commands restoration.
And the God who heals.
Abimelech returned Sarah.
He gave Abraham livestock and servants and permitted him to dwell in the land. Sarah's public standing was addressed.
Then Abraham prayed.
And God healed.
But Genesis gives us one final detail explaining what had been happening behind palace walls.
The Hebrew of Genesis 20:18 reads:
כִּי־עָצֹר עָצַר יְהוָה בְּעַד כָּל־רֶחֶם לְבֵית אֲבִימֶלֶךְ עַל־דְּבַר שָׂרָה אֵשֶׁת אַבְרָהָם
Ki ʿāṣōr ʿāṣar YHWH beʿad kol-reḥem leveit Avimelekh, ʿal-devar Sarah eshet Avraham.
The sense is:
The LORD had completely closed every womb in Abimelech's household because of Sarah, Abraham's wife.
Notice the Hebrew:
עָצֹר עָצַר
ʿāṣōr ʿāṣar.
The same Hebrew root appears twice in an emphatic construction.
The text is intensifying the action.
He had indeed closed.
He had completely restrained.
This was not coincidence masquerading as theology.
The narrator explicitly attributes what happened to YHWH.
And notice another important detail.
The text does not say God hated the women in Abimelech's household.
It does not invite us to create a simplistic doctrine that every case of infertility is divine punishment.
Scripture gives the reason for this particular event because Scripture is describing a particular act of divine intervention.
We should never weaponize Genesis 20 against people experiencing infertility today.
That would go beyond what the passage says and could crush people already carrying enormous grief.
This story tells us what God did there.
It does not authorize us to claim we know why every suffering happens here.
But what happened there was unmistakable.
Sarah had been taken.
God intervened.
The household was afflicted.
Sarah was restored.
Abraham prayed.
God healed.
And then comes one of the most beautiful transitions in Genesis.
Chapter 20 ends with closed wombs.
Chapter 21 begins with Sarah's womb.
After telling us that God healed Abimelech's household, Scripture immediately turns toward the promise God had made to Sarah.
The LORD visited Sarah as He had said.
Sarah conceived.
Isaac was born.
Do you see it?
Closed wombs.
Then an opened womb.
A threatened promise.
Then a fulfilled promise.
Human fear.
Then divine faithfulness.
Scandal.
Then grace.
Abraham nearly created disaster through fear, but Abraham's failure could not make God unfaithful.
This does not excuse Abraham.
Grace never needs to pretend sin was righteous in order to redeem the sinner.
That is one of the most beautiful truths in the Bible.
God does not have to rewrite history by calling darkness light.
He does something better.
He enters ruined stories and brings redemption out of them.
And eventually the story of Abraham, Sarah and Isaac carries us forward toward a far greater Son of promise.
Jesus Christ.
The Bible is not ultimately a collection of moral heroes inviting us to admire how flawless they were.
If it were, Abraham would embarrass the entire project.
So would David.
So would Peter.
So would almost everyone.
And so would we.
Scripture gives us something better than flawless human beings.
It gives us a faithful God.
Generation after generation passes.
Promise after promise unfolds.
Until eventually another promised Child enters human history.
Jesus.
And where Genesis shows God preventing a man from entering deeper into sin, the Gospel shows us something even greater:
God saving sinners who already have.
That is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because maybe your greatest problem isn't what you almost did.
Maybe you did it.
Maybe you crossed the line.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe you destroyed trust.
Maybe pornography owns a room in your life nobody knows exists.
Maybe your marriage looks alive publicly and dead privately.
Maybe bitterness has become so familiar you stopped calling it sin.
Maybe you have been using Christian language while quietly living two lives.
Maybe you cannot read a story about hidden compromise without remembering your own.
Then hear the Gospel carefully.
Jesus did not come only for people who stopped just before the line.
He came for sinners.
Real ones.
Guilty ones.
People with histories.
People with stains.
People whose stories would embarrass them if projected onto the wall of their church.
At the cross, Jesus did not redefine sin until it became harmless.
He demonstrated how serious sin truly is.
And then He bore judgment in the place of sinners.
The sinless Christ died and rose again so that those who repent and believe in Him can receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
That is grace.
Not God saying your sin never mattered.
God saying it mattered so much that redemption required the blood of His Son.
And grace does not merely rescue us from consequences.
Grace begins transforming us.
That is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not religious self-hatred.
It is turning from sin toward God.
It is finally stopping the defense.
Stopping the excuses.
Stopping the hiding.
It is bringing into the light what darkness told you must remain secret forever.
Maybe your prayer today needs fewer impressive words.
Maybe it simply needs to become:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Be honest.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when someone finally stops pretending.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not the only person still fighting to come home.
There is another lesson here we desperately need.
Stop assuming every closed door is rejection.
Abimelech discovered that divine restraint can be mercy.
Some of you are grieving something God would never let happen.
A relationship.
An opportunity.
A plan.
A person.
A future you had already imagined.
We cannot claim that every disappointment is God specifically preventing a particular sin; Scripture does not give us permission to interpret providence that simplistically.
But Genesis 20 does show that God is capable of restraining human beings for their good even when they do not realize He is doing it.
So perhaps your prayer should sometimes change.
Not merely:
“God, open the door.”
But:
“Father, if walking through that door would pull me away from You, love me enough to keep it closed.”
That is a frightening prayer.
It is also freedom.
Because the safest place in the universe is not wherever you get everything you want.
It is wherever Christ has you.
Send it to them.
But financial support can be one voluntary way believers help make biblical teaching and discipleship resources available to others.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not because sharing a post earns spiritual merit.
A Sarah trapped inside consequences she did not create alone.
An Abimelech walking toward a line he does not understand.
A wounded believer convinced their scandal is the final chapter.
Or an unbeliever who has never understood what Christians mean when we say grace.
Let them see it.
God takes sin seriously.
God's warnings are mercy.
God can restrain evil.
God hears prayer.
God restores.
God keeps His promises.
And above everything else, sinners have hope because Jesus Christ died and rose again.
Abraham's failure was not the end.
Sarah's captivity was not the end.
Abimelech's judgment was not the end.
The closed wombs were not the end.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ…
your worst chapter does not have to be the final sentence either.
Because maybe the door God closed wasn't the moment He abandoned you.
Maybe it was the moment mercy stood between you and the story that could have destroyed you.
